title: Benchmark methodology workshop - runtime & KV cache
summary: Workshop focused on establishing a repeatable, apples-to-apples benchmarking methodology for Catalyst Health's inference workloads: defining prompt sets, load generation approaches, caching scenarios (cold/warm), quantization profiles, and on-prem/VPC constraints. Agreed on metric set (p50/p95/p99 latencies, tokens/sec, GPU utilization, memory), artifact sharing, and next steps to run pilot benchmarks on Catalyst dev infra and Redwood Dedicated.

transcript:
Meeting header:
- Date/Time: 2025-05-21 14:00 UTC
- Duration: ~75 minutes
- Attendees: Samir Patel (Redwood AE), Jia Chen (Redwood SE), Luis Ortega (Redwood Solutions Eng), Priya Nair (Redwood Benchmarking Lead); Maya Rao (Catalyst Head of ML), Ethan Kim (Catalyst Platform Eng), Jordan Lee (Catalyst Security), Aaliyah Torres (Catalyst SRE)

Summary (auto): Establishing benchmark methodology for runtime performance tests across hosted/dedicated/private. Focus on prompt selection, load generation, caching scenarios, batching, and quantization.

[00:00] Samir: hey everyone thanks for joining, i think we have about an hour and fifteen, we'll run through methodology + hands on bench plan. priya from our team will drive the harness discussion.
[00:22] Maya: thanks, we wanted this because our dashboards show inconsistent p95s across models and we need a repeatable approach to evaluate tradeoffs — especially when we consider dedicated vs vpc/on-prem deployments.
[00:35] Jia: cool; high level we'll align on: prompt corpus (seed set vs long tail), load generation (rps vs concurrency vs target tokens/sec), warm vs cold kv cache, batch size strategies, and quantization profiles. then we can run an apples-to-apples run.
[00:48] Ethan: short question — when you say apples-to-apples, do you mean same model weights, same tokenizer, same batch settings, same sequence length distribution?
[01:02] Priya: yes exactly. apples-to-apples means same model config (same checkpoint/quantization), same tokenizer and truncation rules, identical input distribution. also same inference harness (no client-side batching differences). that avoids measuring differences due to harness.
[01:20] Jordan: and from security side we need the harness to run within our VPC or at least within a controlled subnet — we can't route raw logs externally.
[01:30] Samir: understood. we'll share a dockerized bench agent that can be deployed into your subnet and will upload only metrics (no raw prompts) or encrypted artifacts per your spec.
[01:45] Aaliyah: can you run on-prem too? we have racks with A100s and a mix of T4s for dev.
[01:53] Luis: yes we support dedicated + private deployments. for on-prem we usually run the same harness — only difference is network latency to control plane and filesystem speeds; we'll capture those.
[02:10] [02:10] Maya: let's dig into prompt sets — we have short completion prompts (like search rewrite) and long document summarization. How should we structure test cases?
[02:25] Priya: we recommend three buckets: micro (<= 64 tokens), mid (65–512 tokens), macro (>512 tokens). for each bucket supply representative prompts and expected output length. also include a tail set with random real queries. keep a stable seed corpus for regression tests and a randomized augmentation for stress tests.
[02:44] Jia: important detail — tokenization differences matter. if you're comparing models from different families or quantization alters tokenization, you must normalize by tokenizer version and pre-tokenize inputs to get exact token counts.
[02:59] Ethan: noted. for load gen, should we drive by concurrency or by rps? we saw weird autoscaling behavior when we used rps alone.
[03:10] Priya: drive by target concurrency distribution and target tokens/sec. rps can be misleading because varying sequence length changes token throughput. we suggest specifying a sequence length histogram and desired tail p99 tokens/sec.
[03:28] Samir: we'll provide a harness that takes a sequence length distribution and target throughput; harness will simulate client arrival patterns (poisson, bursty).
[03:40] [03:40] Jordan: what about KV cache? our real workload has a lot of repeated prefixes from patient records, so cache hit rate matters.
[03:52] Luis: KV cache changes latency dramatically for long context retrievals. for apples-to-apples you should run both cold-cache (start of day) and warm-cache (after synthetic warming) passes. measure both absolute latencies and delta. also record cache hit ratio and per-request cache usage.
[04:12] Priya: also measure how cache eviction policies interact with batching; for example if the harness simulates many small conversations, cache churn can reduce hit rate. consider longer-lived conversation ids during warm runs.
[04:30] Maya: quantization — we have compliance constraints so int8 is attractive for cost but worried about quality regressions and latency artifacts. what's realistic?
[04:42] Jia: quantization reduces memory plus can improve throughput but also sometimes increases latency per token due to dequant/decode overhead depending on kernel implementations. our recommendation: test at FP32/FP16/int8 and collect both latency and output-similarity metrics (perplexity, embedding cosine on a sample set, or RLHF eval if available).
[05:05] [05:05] Ethan: are there standard quality thresholds you recommend? like max 2% embedding delta or something?
[05:12] Priya: often teams set thresholds per use case. for retrieval/embedding, 0.5–1% cosine drop might be acceptable; for generation tasks you may use automated evals plus spot human checks. capture BLEU/ROUGE/embedding back-compat.
[05:28] Samir: note that latency SLOs are also important — show p95 and p99. we often see FP16 improves p50 but p99 can get worse under contention if memory pressure forces spill. so collect GPU utilization, mem alloc failures, and retry counts.
[05:50] [05:50] Maya: how to ensure identical model weights? when we test dedicated vs hosted, sometimes there's slight build-time differences.
[05:59] Luis: pin exact checkpoint hashes and include a checksum of the model binary and the tokenizer. version your kernel stack (CUDA, cuDNN, runtime). produce an artifacts.json with exact versions.
[06:18] Jia: also include deterministic seed for non-deterministic ops where possible. for sampling tasks use same temperature/top-k seeds and compare using the same decoding algorithm (greedy vs nucleus).
[06:35] [06:35] Ethan: batching strategy differences — what do you recommend? micro-batching vs large batches?
[06:42] Priya: benchmark across a sweep: single-request (batch=1), small batches (2–8), medium (16–64), large (128+) depending on GPU memory. measure latency tail and throughput. Importantly, test continuous batching (runtime can aggregate requests) vs client-side fixed batches. Redwood's runtime does continuous batching and that can change latency curves versus fixed batching.
[07:05] Samir: we'll capture per-batch size metrics in harness. one tip: when reporting token/sec, also show tokens-per-gpu-second to normalize across hardware.
[07:22] [07:22] Jordan: network effects for VPC/on-prem — should we simulate cross-AZ traffic?
[07:30] Luis: yes. for private deployments, measure control-plane roundtrips and any NFS/filestore latency if loading weights. also test cold-start times for model pull and KV cache warm time especially when models are swapped.
[07:45] Maya: we also care about model switching in rollouts — like canary vs full — and how warm cache behaves.
[07:52] Jia: include a canary ramp test: start at 5% traffic for 10 minutes then 20% then 100% while capturing latency deltas; this shows cache warming impact on rollout strategy.
[08:05] [08:05] Ethan: instrumentation — what exporters do you use? prometheus? tracing?
[08:12] Samir: we recommend prometheus for metrics and jaeger/opentelemetry for traces. harness will export metrics to a pushgateway or local prom endpoint; we can also send traces with redaction. all exports can be disabled if you can't allow egress.
[08:26] Priya: add synthetic request IDs to measure per-conversation latency; export KV cache hit metrics and per-batch GPU utilization (nvidia-smi or DCGM).
[08:37] [08:37] Maya: can you summarize the canonical metric set we should capture?
[08:42] Priya: sure: p50/p90/p95/p99 latency (ms), tokens/sec overall, tokens/sec per GPU, GPU utilization (%), GPU memory usage (peak & avg), cache hit rate, model load time (cold), cache warm time, error/retry counts, output quality metrics (embedding cosine or automated scores).
[09:05] Samir: and include system-level metrics: CPU io wait, network latency, filesystem throughput for on-prem.
[09:12] [09:12] Maya: about output quality, we need a small human-in-loop evaluation for the summarization set. can Redwood help run an eval?
[09:22] Luis: we can provide an eval harness and suggested rubric; but for PHI or sensitive data you should scrub or provide synthetic data. we can run on scrubbed data.
[09:33] [09:33] Ethan: let's talk about load generation specifics — burstiness, poisson, steady-state. what do you recommend for realistic retail-ish traffic?
[09:44] Priya: use a mixture. 70% steady-state with poisson arrivals, 20% small bursts (10–30x for short periods), 10% long tails. simulate peak windows with ramps. specify client-side timeouts identical across tests to avoid hiding tail latencies via retries.
[10:04] [10:04] Jordan: for compliance we need logs to be truncated and anonymized. can the harness mask PII before any metric export?
[10:12] Samir: yes harness can hash prompts and only export hashes; raw prompts never leave your VPC unless you opt-in. we'll provide config toggles.
[10:22] [10:22] Maya: what about load from multiple clients with multiplexed KV namespaces? our product has multitenant prefixes.
[10:30] Jia: simulate multi-namespace traffic by assigning conversation IDs to namespaces and measuring cross-namespace cache isolation effects. also test eviction when namespaces compete for cache memory.
[10:45] [10:45] Ethan: can we see an example benchmark plan?
[10:50] Priya: yes i'll outline a plan: 1) baseline single-request micro test across FP32/FP16/int8; 2) warm vs cold cache pass; 3) batch-sweep; 4) arrival-pattern sweep (steady, bursty); 5) canary ramp test; 6) long-run stability (4–8 hours) to observe mem leaks. each step uses the same prompt corpus and artifacts.json pinned versions.
[11:15] Samir: also note environmental reproducibility — container images, kernel params, and ML runtime versions. record everything.
[11:25] [11:25] Maya: on the apples-to-apples comparators, what about comparing hosted Redwood to their hosted competitor? they will argue network differences.
[11:33] Luis: if you want apples-to-apples against a managed provider, run the workload from the same client location and pre-tokenize inputs. for hosted-to-hosted compare tokens/sec per model at the same checkpoint & quantization. for on-prem vs hosted, normalize by hardware (tokens/GPU-second).
[11:50] Priya: include cost-per-token calc too so tradeoffs are clear. show p95 latency vs $/1000 tokens.
[12:02] [12:02] Ethan: any gotchas with quantization and KV cache interactions?
[12:08] Jia: quantized kernels may change memory layout of activations; some runtimes change KV cache packing which can affect memory throughput and eviction behavior. test both together.
[12:22] Maya: scheduling — we need to coordinate windows when we can run heavy benchmarks on our infra. can we schedule low-priority runs overnight?
[12:30] Samir: yes harness supports scheduling and load caps; we'll work with Ethan to pick windows.
[12:40] Luis: final note — when we report results, we'll include confidence intervals and raw traces so you can reproduce.
[12:50] [12:50] Maya: ok recap?
[12:54] Samir: recap: share harness + prompt corpus, Catalyst shares traces and histograms, schedule on-prem pilot week of 2025-06-02, run baseline FP32/FP16/int8 and warm/cold cache passes, compare tokens/gpu-sec and p95/p99, and produce a cost-latency tradeoff chart.
[13:12] Maya: thanks all. Ethan and Jordan will coordinate infra and security.
[13:20] Samir: thanks, we'll follow up in email with repo link and runbook.
